Split a Surname and Given Name Written as One Word

Source: R/split_run_together.R
split_run_together.Rd

Some records run a person's surname and given name together: KramerKenneth, LedbetterJennifer A, MURPHYSANDRA. split_run_together() puts the space back when the evidence is strong, and leaves every other name alone. The parser's order rules then decide which part is the surname, as for any other name.

Usage

split_run_together(x)

Arguments

x

A character vector of raw names.

Value

x, with a space inserted where a run-together word was split.

Details

Two rules, both requiring that the whole word is not itself a name in census.names:

  • A capital letter inside a word (KramerKenneth): split at the capital when both parts have at least three letters, one is mostly a surname and the other mostly a given name in the census (at least 80% of 500 or more records), and the first part is not a surname particle (McDonald, MacArthur, DeShawn, LaToya, VanDyke and similar are left alone).

  • All capitals (MURPHYSANDRA): only when the word is the name's one word of two or more letters (other words are initials, titles or suffixes), has at least eight letters, and splits into a strong surname (95% of 2,000 or more records) and a strong given name (95% of 20,000 or more records), each of four or more letters. Words that recur in many different Form 990 names (MARKWALD, PEARLSTONE, GLENFIELD) are real surnames and are never split.

The all-capitals rule is the riskier of the two: a rare surname can look like two common names. That is why parse_names() runs neither rule unless asked (split_run_together = TRUE).

See also

vignette("name-types")

Examples

split_run_together(c("KramerKenneth", "LedbetterJennifer A", "MURPHYSANDRA",
                     "McDonald", "LaToya Smith", "JOHN MARKWALD", "MARKWALD J"))
#> [1] "Kramer Kenneth"       "Ledbetter Jennifer A" "MURPHY SANDRA"       
#> [4] "McDonald"             "LaToya Smith"         "JOHN MARKWALD"       
#> [7] "MARKWALD J"
